title: Users, Tenants, and Permissions
readerIntent: Understand how Nodics represents people, organizations, non-human callers, and access without requiring source-code knowledge.
owner: Profile identity records, nAuth credential security, and authorization in each target module
summary: Nodics separates tenant and enterprise context, employee and customer identities, service principals, groups, permissions, record ownership, and target-module policy so every caller receives only the intended access.

sections.heading: Business model
items: Tenant is the isolation and configuration boundary for an application deployment.
Enterprise represents a governed organization inside the supported tenant model; parent enterprise relationships may express business hierarchy.
Employee is a human permitted to use business and BackOffice capabilities.
Customer is a human consumer whose access is normally constrained to owned records and consumer operations.
Service principal represents a module, integration, or controlled scheduled process and never signs in with a person's password.

sections.heading: How access is decided
items: Authentication proves the principal and credential are currently trusted.
Token type and audience prevent human, customer, and service credentials from becoming interchangeable.
Groups compose catalogued permissions through validated, active, acyclic inheritance.
The target route checks exposure, token class, permission, and tenant context.
The target schema and service check action, fields, ownership, relationships, and business state.
A caller may narrow trusted context but cannot broaden it by sending different tenant, enterprise, owner, or relationship values.

sections.heading: Administrative guidance
items: Grant the smallest groups and permissions needed for a role.
Keep customer registration from accepting privileged groups, permissions, API keys, or service-only state.
Use user-friendly names in administrative interfaces while preserving stable codes for contracts.
Review inactive users, inherited access, service credentials, cross-tenant permissions, and security-stamp invalidation regularly.
Use governed migration, audit, rotation, and rollback for identity-policy changes.
